title: At most N at a time

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo sends reminder emails through a fake mail service that refuses more than three connections at once.

tasks.title: Send in batches
tasks.description:
Implement `runInBatches(items, size, fn)` in `src/batches.js`. It calls `fn(item, index)` for every item, `size` items at a time: start a whole batch, wait until every call in it has finished, then start the next batch.

- `index` is the item's position in the whole list
- resolve with every result, in the same order as `items`
- the last batch may be smaller
- if a call rejects, reject with that error and start no further batches
- an empty list resolves with `[]` without calling `fn`

**Timing:** there is no clock here. `fn` is the slow work, and the check passes a fake job whose calls it settles by hand, one at a time, recording which items had started after each step.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and read the first line.
Loop over the list in steps of `size`.
Run each slice at once and wait for all of it before moving on.
Run the demo again and compare its time with the next line's later on.
hints: This is a loop where each turn handles one slice of the list, and the turns happen one after the other.
`items.slice(start, start + size)` gives you one batch. You already know a way to wait for several promises at once.
Inside an async function, `await Promise.all(batch.map(...))` per turn of a `for` loop does it. Remember to add `start` to the index within the batch.

tasks.title: Keep the line moving
tasks.description:
Implement `mapLimit(items, limit, fn)` in `src/mapLimit.js`. It calls `fn(item, index)` for every item with at most `limit` calls in flight, and starts the next item as soon as **any** call finishes, without waiting for the rest of a batch.

- start items in list order
- resolve with every result, in the same order as `items`
- with fewer items than `limit`, start them all at once
- an empty list resolves with `[]` without calling `fn`
- if a call rejects, reject with that error, start no new items after it, and leave no rejection unhandled

**Timing:** there is no clock here. The check passes a fake job whose calls it settles by hand in an order it chooses, and records which items had started after each step and the most calls in flight at once.
nextSteps: Decide how you will remember which item comes next.
Write a small async loop that takes the next item, runs it and repeats.
Run `limit` of those loops side by side and wait for them all.
Run the demo: the limited line should be faster than batches.
hints: Think of `limit` workers sharing one queue. Each worker takes the next item, waits for it, then takes another, until the queue is empty.
A shared `next` counter that each worker reads and increments gives you the index. Store each result at `results[index]` so the order is kept.
Start `Math.min(limit, items.length)` workers and wait for them with `Promise.all`. On a failure, set a flag that makes every worker stop taking new items, and rethrow.

tasks.title: Finish the list even when some fail
tasks.description:
Implement `mapLimitSettled(items, limit, fn)` in `src/mapLimitSettled.js`. It has the same limit and order as `mapLimit`, but a failed item does not stop the others and the result never rejects. It resolves with one entry per item, in order:

- `{ ok: true, value }` when `fn(item, index)` resolved
- `{ ok: false, error }` when it rejected, where `error` is the rejection itself, not its message

**Timing:** there is no clock here. The check passes a fake job whose calls it settles by hand and records which items had started after each failure and the most calls in flight at once.
nextSteps: Decide what a failed reminder should turn into.
Wrap `fn` so that it never rejects.
Run the demo and find B9 in the last line.
hints: `mapLimit` already keeps the limit and the order. It only stops when a job rejects.
If every job resolves, `mapLimit` never stops early. What if a job's failure were turned into a value?
Pass `mapLimit` an async function that awaits `fn(item, index)` inside try and catch, and returns `{ ok: true, value }` or `{ ok: false, error }`.
